frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d372:
Minutes kept by Ware record a Tehran conversation of 30 November 1943, at half past one, among Harry Hopkins, Anthony Eden, and Soviet foreign minister Molotov. Its subject is the strong points the victorious powers would hold after the war, and the punishment of France.

Molotov names Bizerte and Dakar and asks after Bizerte's sovereignty, arguing the war must affect such places, as Stalin also holds. Hopkins raises Belgium and Holland, too close to Germany to defend themselves. Molotov answers that France is a different case: she did not merely fall, she would not defend herself and now actively supports German strategy. Eden concedes nothing is too bad for the Lavals and Pétains. On bases in friendly countries, Eden offers the West Indies bases-for-ships deal as a rough model, while Hopkins resists his suggestion that affection explained it.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d472:
President Roosevelt, then at Cairo, sent a message to Secretary of State Cordell Hull in Washington on December 3, 1943. It was the eve of the Second Cairo Conference, and Roosevelt had just come from the Tehran meeting with Stalin and Churchill. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

The President and his Secretary of State were separated by an ocean for the whole summit season, so their traffic carried real weight: reports on the talks, instructions, and decisions sent home. This message is one strand of that wire. It reminds readers that the conferences ran on cables as much as on handshakes.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d572:

By then Harry Truman was president, Roosevelt having died in April, and Leahy served the new President in the same post. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Germany had surrendered three weeks earlier, and the machinery built at Tehran and Cairo was being turned toward Japan and the peace. A Leahy message to the Secretary of State carried the White House's military-political view in its most direct form. For readers, it shows the wartime staff system surviving its founder and serving his successor.

frus-1944-quebec-d272:

The world body items lead the list. On Council voting, Stettinius backs a formula of seven votes, including the permanent members. A party to a dispute would not vote on peaceful settlement. Other items cover first membership and a headquarters district on Swiss and French soil near Geneva. Study of trusteeships, drafting the court statute, and ending the League of Nations round out the page.

The Zetetic was a journal of the flat-earth movement, and this file holds its very first issue: volume 1, number 1, dated July 1872, edited by Chas. Brough. Zetetic astronomy taught that the earth is a flat plane and that direct experience, not authority, settles such questions.

The flat-earth cause in Victorian Britain ran through periodicals like this one, passed among committed believers. The issue survives as the debut of the movement's own press.
fergusson-rude-stone-monuments-1872:
Architectural historian James Fergusson surveyed rough stone monuments across the world in 1872. His book asks two plain questions: how old are they, and what were they for? Circles, rows, and tombs all fall in his scope.

He compares sites in Britain, India, Africa, and beyond. His drawings and plans give the book lasting use. Fergusson argues against wild claims of vast age for many sites. Some views are dated, as with all Victorian surveys. Still, the round-up remains a base reference for anyone who studies megaliths in bulk. His scope alone still commands real respect.
preston-illustrations-of-masonry-1772:
William Preston, a Scottish printer turned London Mason, published Illustrations of Masonry at London in 1772. The first edition is the base text of the modern Masonic lecture system. Preston wrote for a craft then meeting in taverns and moving toward grand temples.

The book prints the craft's rites, its formal talks for each degree, and its songs. It also gives the first printed history of Masonry, tracing the craft back through the ages. Preston's clear order shaped how lodges taught their members for the next hundred years. Few books have done more to fix a craft's shared practice in print.
evans-ancient-stone-implements-1872:
John Evans, a paper manufacturer and antiquary, published The Ancient Stone Implements, Weapons, and Ornaments of Great Britain in 1872. Evans had helped prove human antiquity in the Somme gravels beside Boucher de Perthes. His book is the typology of British stone tools, the sorting of them by form and age.

Spears, axes, scrapers, and ornaments are drawn and described piece by piece. Evans gave archaeologists their working vocabulary: hand-axe, scraper, and burin are used worldwide still. The book made flint study a science with standards of proof. Its plates remain handsome, and its judgments careful. For British prehistory, it is the reference the Victorians built on.
darwin-expression-of-emotions-1872:
Charles Darwin published The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals in 1872. He asked why faces and bodies show feeling in such similar ways worldwide. Photographs and engravings of faces, including infants and animals, illustrate his points.

Darwin argues that expressions are inherited habits, not separately created gifts. Smiles, frowns, blushes, and bared teeth all get close attention. The book followed his works on species and human descent. It founded the scientific study of emotion and still reads with surprising freshness. He gathered evidence through letters from travelers, missionaries, and doctors around the world.
owen-debatable-land-1872:
Robert Dale Owen walks the edge twixt worlds once more in The Debatable Land, his book of 1872. His first book on the theme had made his name in 1860. Here he goes past tales to claims: what the dead are, how they speak, and what their words mean for how we live and what we hold dear.

Fresh cases and long thought fill the tome. Owen writes as a man of state, not a cult chief. His calm won fans who shunned wild tracts. The book was the most cited work of its kind from his land.
cox-spiritualism-answered-science-1872:
Edward Cox, a high law man, weighed the seance in Spiritualism Answered by Science, out in 1872. Cox held the rank of Serjeant in the courts of London. He ran his own tests with the seers of the day, Home midst them, in rooms he set and watched with a law man's eye for proof and its flaws.

He grants strange force, yet balks at ghosts. A mind force, he claims, not the dead, moves the goods. That mid stand made his book a mark. It is the law's cool word on the theme.
nostradamus-true-prophecies-garencieres-:
Theophilus de Garencieres, a French doctor who lived in London, turned Nostradamus into English in 1672. His was the first full English text of the famed French seer. The book also holds a long preface on the seer's life and times. That life tale was read as fact in England for a long span of years.

The verses run in their set order, with notes to help the reader through hard lines. Garencieres kept the dark tone of the French while he made the words plain English. His text fixed Nostradamus in the English mind as a true prophet for years to come.
bastian-beginnings-of-life-1872:
Henry Charlton Bastian, a London doctor, made his case for life from dead stuff in this two part work of 1872. He named his scheme heterogenesis, birth from unlike stuff. By then Pasteur's proof had won most of the field, but Bastian held his ground.

Bastian set out trials in which, he claimed, sealed flasks grew life from pure fluids. He was a skilled man, and his books gave the old claim its last fair case in print. Tyndall and Pasteur took up his trials and showed the flaw, step by step, in the years that came.
virchow-neanderthal-1872:
Rudolf Virchow, the great German doctor, gave his report on the Neanderthal skull in German in 1872. He was the most feared voice in the study of the body in his age. His word on a bone could make or break a claim for years to come.

Virchow held that the skull was that of a sick and bent modern man, not an old race. Disease, he said, had warped the brow and limbs in life, and age had done the rest. That word from such a height held back the Neanderthal claim for a long span of years.
strindberg-master-olof-1872:
August Strindberg wrote Master Olof in 1872, his breakthrough historical drama, here in Edwin Björkman's translation. The play of his youth tells of Olaus Petri and the Swedish Reformation under Gustav Vasa in Sweden. He reworked it for years, in verse and prose, before the stage would take it at last.

Young Olof, a priest afire with Luther's doctrine, defies bishops and his own mother for reform. King Gustav uses the new faith to break Rome and seize church wealth for the crown of Sweden. Olof joins a failed plot, recants to save his life, and ends tamed as the king's servant. The drama asks what a reformer owes truth when power offers him a pulpit on terms. Björkman's version brought Strindberg's first major play to English readers and stages abroad.
daudet-tartarin-tarascon-1872:
Alphonse Daudet published Tartarin of Tarascon in 1872, here in the English translation of 1896 in print. The comic masterpiece sends a blowhard Provençal lion-hunter to his Saharan misadventures in colonial Algeria of the day. Daudet loved Provence and mocked it in one breath, and Tartarin is his fondest, funniest creation in prose.

Tartarin, fat and boastful, talks of lions until his town shames him into sailing for Africa. In Algiers he shoots a donkey, a blind beggar's lion, and lands in plots of fake princes. His Sancho-like servant and his own tall tales keep the farce warm rather than cruel in Daudet's hands. He returns home a hero on the strength of one old, tame, and much disputed lion. The book made the Tarascon type, the southern braggart with a golden heart, immortal in French humor.
andersen-fairy-tales-1872:
Hans Christian Andersen's Fairy Tales appear here in the classic English translation of his immortal Danish tales. The mermaid, the snow queen, the ugly duckling, and the steadfast tin soldier people this beloved set of stories. Andersen, a shoemaker's son from Odense, published his first tales for children in 1835.

The Little Mermaid trades her voice for legs and dissolves into sea foam for love of a prince. The Snow Queen sends Gerda through seasons and robbers to melt Kai's frozen heart with her warm tears of love. The Ugly Duckling, read as Andersen's own life, turns scorn and winter into a swan's spring at last. His tales, unlike the Grimms', were invented, not collected, and their melancholy is a poet's own in every line. In the classic English dress here, they formed the nursery canon of the English-speaking world.
hernandez-martin-fierro-1872:
Jose Hernandez published Martin Fierro in 1872, a long poem in Spanish about a gaucho on the Argentine pampas. Fierro is a singer and horseman who is forced into army service on the frontier. He deserts, loses his home and family, and becomes an outlaw. A second part, published later, follows his return.

Fierro tells his story in song, in the voice of the payada tradition. He speaks of hard work, unfair laws, and loyalty among friends. The poem became the national epic of Argentina. It is still read as a defense of the gaucho way of life against a changing state.
verne-around-world-1872:
Jules Verne published Around the World in Eighty Days in 1872, a novel built around a wager. Phileas Fogg bets that he can circle the globe in eighty days. He sets out from London with his servant Passepartout. Trains, ships, and stagecoaches carry them across four continents.

Delays, arrests, and rescues keep the race tense to the final hours. A detective who thinks Fogg is a thief follows them the whole way. In India they save a young woman, Aouda, who joins the trip. The ending turns on a neat trick of time and travel. The book remains a model of the well-made adventure.
hodge-systematic-theology-vol1-1872:
Charles Hodge taught at Princeton Seminary for more than fifty years and made it the stronghold of Calvinist teaching in America. His Systematic Theology, Volume 1, came out in 1872. It opens his great system with first principles, the doctrine of God, and the doctrine of man.

Hodge says theology gathers its facts from the Bible the way a student of nature gathers facts from the world. This volume treats how we can know God, his nature and perfections, the Trinity, creation, and the fall of man. Students at Princeton learned their faith from Hodge, and his clear definitions shaped Presbyterian teaching in America for years.
legge-chinese-classics-vol-5-part-1-1872:
James Legge published Volume 5, Part 1 of The Chinese Classics in 1872. The text is the Ch'un Ts'ew, the Spring and Autumn Annals, a terse chronicle of the state of Lu. Tradition ascribed the Annals to Confucius himself, and Chinese scholars read deep moral judgments into its spare words.

Part 1 gives the Chinese text with Legge's translation and notes, the first English version of the Annals. Entries record births, deaths, battles, and eclipses in a few dry words each. Legge's prolegomena, his long opening study, explained the text, its commentaries, and its history. The dryness is the point: readers see the seed from which centuries of commentary grew.
legge-chinese-classics-vol-5-part-2-1872:
Volume 5, Part 2 of Legge's Chinese Classics appeared in 1872, completing his Spring and Autumn Annals. James Legge, the Scottish scholar of China, paired the Annals with the Tso Chuan, the great commentary that turns the dry chronicle into narrative. Part 1 had introduced the Annals themselves.

The Tso Chuan tells the stories behind the Annals' bare entries: speeches, battles, plots, and the fall of states. Legge translated the commentary with notes drawn from Chinese scholars. With this part, English readers could read both the record and its classic explanation together. The volume completed Legge's five-volume Chinese Classics, the foundation of Chinese studies in English for a century.
turgenev-torrents-of-spring-1872:
The Torrents of Spring, Turgenev's novella of 1872, comes in Constance Garnett's English. Dimitri Sanin, traveling in Frankfurt as a young man, saves a pastry shop from ruin and falls for Gemma, its owner's daughter. He sells his estate to marry her and seal their future together.

Sent to close the sale with a rich Russian lady, Sanin falls under her spell in a single day. He betrays Gemma, loses her, and spends his life in regret. The older Sanin tells the tale after finding a garnet cross that recalls it all. Turgenev shapes the story with perfect economy. Many readers judge it his most flawless short novel.
bishops-bible-1572:
Archbishop Matthew Parker led a team of bishops to revise the Great Bible, and their Bishops' Bible first appeared in 1568. The 1572 edition given here was the Bible ordered to be read in parish churches across England. It held that place until the King James version replaced it in 1611.

The translators of King James took the Bishops' Bible as their base text, by royal command, so its wording lives on inside the famous version. The print of 1572 is grand, with woodcuts and large type for the lectern. The text here was transcribed from a facsimile scan, and the spelling is rough in places. It remains a key stage in the story of the English Bible.
ibn-al-athir-kamel-rhc-1872:
Ibn al-Athir chronicled the Crusades from the Muslim side in his Kamil, excerpted here in the French Recueil of 1872. The great Mosul historian's al-Kamil fi'l-ta'rikh, his Complete History, covers the Frankish wars from 1098 to 1231 in this extract. Tome I of the Historiens orientaux gave French readers the eastern voice on events the West usually tells alone.

Sieges, truces, and the rise of Saladin pass in annal form, year by year. Ibn al-Athir judges the Franks shrewdly and his own princes harshly when they divided. The extract remains a first source for the Crusades, precious for its outside view.
maxwell-theory-of-heat-1872:
James Clerk Maxwell wrote his Theory of Heat in 1872 as a plain textbook for students. Maxwell was already famous for his work on electricity and light. Here he turns to a humbler topic: what heat is, and how it moves.

The book explains temperature, conduction, and the way gases behave when warmed or squeezed. Maxwell shows how tiny moving particles can explain the pressure and heat of a gas. His famous thought experiment about a sorting 'demon' also appears here, and it still sparks debate about order and chance. Teachers used it for years as a first guide to the subject.
allibone-critical-dictionary-english-lit:
Volume Two of Allibone's Critical Dictionary appeared in 1872, fourteen years after the first, covering K to Q. Samuel Allibone had spent the interval gathering still more notices. The delay shows in the volume's fullness.

Entries continue the pattern: brief lives, full lists of writings, and quoted opinions from the press. American authors receive generous space beside their British cousins. Allibone's own judgments are plain and sometimes sharp, in the manner of a working bookseller. The middle volume carries the dictionary through the heart of the alphabet, a reference no literary library of the age lacked.
stanley-how-i-found-livingstone-1872:
Henry Stanley, a Welsh-born reporter for the New York Herald, was sent in 1871 to find David Livingstone, lost in Africa. How I Found Livingstone, from 1872, is his bestseller about the search. It made Stanley the most famous explorer-reporter alive.

His caravan fought fever, floods, deserters, and hostile chiefs across East Africa. At Ujiji on Lake Tanganyika he met the gaunt old missionary with the famous words, 'Dr Livingstone, I presume?' The greeting became legend, though Stanley later cut the page from his diary. The book mixes fine reporting with self-promotion, and it launched African exploration's most driven career.
plos-pone-0003372:
Stuart J. McDougall and co-authors tackled a lab measurement problem in this 2008 paper. They worked with isoflurane, a gas used to put patients and animals to sleep. The gas fades fast in open lab dishes, so the true dose is hard to know. The team paired dose checks with recordings from nerve connections.

Their method measured the real gas level in the dish at the same time as nerve signals. That pairing let them match each dose to its true effect on synapses. Honest dose data matters because sleep drugs are judged by dose and response curves. The approach gives other labs a cleaner way to test gases like this one.
plos-pone-0003472:
Kenneth C. Catania studied a Florida folk trade in this 2008 paper. Families near Apalachicola National Forest earn money gathering large earthworms for bait. They drive a wooden stake into the soil and vibrate it. The giant worms then crawl to the surface on their own.

Catania argued the trick mimics a digging mole, the worms' predator. Worms flee upward to escape what they take for a hunter. People have used the method for generations without knowing why it works. The paper ties folk practice to a neat piece of animal behavior.
plos-pone-0003572:
Christopher D. Wiley and co-authors studied gene imprinting in hybrid deer mice in this 2008 paper. Imprinting silences one parent's copy of certain genes. Crosses between two Peromyscus species disturb growth and development. One cross direction gave growth-retarded but healthy offspring.

In hybrids, imprinting was lost in tissue- and cluster-specific patterns. Which parent a copy came from mattered differently by tissue. The patchwork shows imprinting is regulated locally. No single genome-wide rule explains the losses. Deer mice are a common wild model for how genes and parents shape growth. The two species can still breed, which makes the contrast sharper.
plos-pone-0003672:
Michelle M. Riehle, Jiannong Xu, Brian P. Lazzaro, and colleagues published this malaria study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Earlier mapping had found a stretch of the Anopheles gambiae mosquito genome that sways infection outcomes. The team hunted the genes inside that region using the rodent malaria parasite.

They identified APL1, a family of varied proteins built from leucine-rich repeats. APL1 proved required for protection driven by the Rel1 pathway against Plasmodium berghei. The finding names mosquito immune genes that help decide whether a bite can pass malaria on to a person.
plos-pone-0003772:
Cristina Mazzaccara, Giuseppe Labruna, Gennaro Cito, and colleagues published this reference study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The mouse is the most used animal model for human disease. Yet reference values for blood tests were scanty for the strains labs use most. The team set out to fill that gap.

They measured the main biochemical and blood cell parameters in three strains: C57BL/6J, 129SV/EV, and C3H/HeJ. Values are given by age, so normal change over a mouse's life is not mistaken for disease. The tables give researchers baselines for spotting real effects in experiments.
plos-pone-0003872:
Magdalini Polymenidou, Rita Moos, Mike Scott, and co-authors described a set of lab tools for prion research in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article centers on the prion protein and its harmful folded form. That folded form builds up in prion disease and drives damage to the brain. Studying it requires antibodies that bind to known spots on the protein.

The team built a set of monoclonal antibodies called the POM series. Each antibody binds a different spot, and the spots do not overlap. Together they cover the prion protein in a planned way. Other labs can use the set to detect the protein and probe how it changes.
plos-pone-0003972:
William E. Banks, Francesco d'Errico, A. Townsend Peterson, and co-authors modeled Neanderthal extinction in 2008. Debate has long split between climate change and competition as the cause. Modern humans spread as Neanderthals vanished from Europe. The authors brought a new method to the old question.

Their PLOS ONE article joins archaeological and dating data with climate models. The results support extinction by competitive exclusion by modern humans. In that view, two groups cannot long share one niche. The study weighs evidence toward rivalry rather than weather alone. Readers can find the full text in PLOS ONE, an open science journal.
plos-pone-0004072:
Robert Reiner, Natalie Krasnov-Yoeli, Yana Dehtiar, and co-authors studied a chromatin-bound enzyme complex in 2008. Human RNase P was first known for trimming transfer RNA. It is built from an RNA called H1 plus at least ten proteins. Newer findings tied it to transcription of small RNA genes.

Their PLOS ONE article examines RNase P attached to chromatin. That form is required for efficient transcription by RNA polymerase I. One complex thus serves both RNA processing and gene transcription. The dual role reshapes how this classic enzyme is understood. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004172:
Jung Boo and colleagues published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Presenilin is a protein involved in many cell events in health and disease. Earlier reports found that cells lacking presenilin grow too fast and resist the normal process of cell death.

The team asked how presenilin loss affects one specific death route: damage from reactive oxygen species, the harmful molecules called ROS. They report that phosphorylated beta-catenin, a signalling protein, builds up in the deficient cells and makes ROS-driven death stronger. The finding complicates the picture of presenilin loss as simply protective, and it matters for diseases where presenilin fails, including Alzheimer's.
plos-pone-0004272:
Emilie Sapin and colleagues published this sleep neuroanatomy study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Paradoxical sleep, also called REM sleep, brings a busy cortex, rapid eye movements, and limp muscles. Fifty years after its discovery, the neuronal network that generates it was still only partly identified.

The team had proposed that GABAergic neurons, cells using the inhibitory signal GABA, hold the key. Here they localise the brainstem GABAergic neurons that control paradoxical sleep. Pinpointing the switch for the dreaming state brings a half-century-old map closer to completion. The brainstem is the stalk that links the brain and the spinal cord.
plos-pone-0004372:
Ulf Meyer-Hoffert, Zhihong Wu, and Jens-Michael Schröder published this skin study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Kallikrein-related peptidases are serine proteases involved in desquamation, the shedding of skin. Their activity is tightly controlled by epidermal protease inhibitors such as LEKTI, and defects in the LEKTI gene cause severe skin disease.

The team report finding lympho-epithelial Kazal-type inhibitor 2 in human skin. They report that it is a specific inhibitor of kallikrein-related peptidase 5. Naming a dedicated brake for one skin protease refines the picture of how skin renews itself without digesting itself. Skin sheds its outer layer every day, so the brakes matter constantly.
plos-pone-0004472: In 2009, Pesendorfer, Gunhold, and Schiel found monkeys keeping habits, not copying. Marmoset traditions persisted through individual habit, not social conformity. The field experiment settled the debate cleanly. The finding nuances culture's deep roots. The monkeys foraged alone in their style.
plos-pone-0004572: In 2009, Koschwanez, Carlson, and Meldrum thinned silicone films for lab chips. Thin PDMS films were made using long spin times or tert-butyl alcohol. The solvent swap beat nasty hexane. The method aids lab-on-a-chip building today. The films are flexible.
plos-pone-0004672: In 2009, Kranjc, Grillo, and Rievaj modeled a newly found chloride channel family anew here. Regulation of bestrophins by Ca2+ was studied theoretically and experimentally. The channels opened with rising calcium. The paper informs channel biology today. The family is recent.
plos-pone-0004772: In 2009, Sanz and a team found a virus reading its message two ways. A dual trick for reading short mRNA from Sindbis virus was found. The sick cells shut down host making. The study maps viral reading. The shutdown halt is deep.
zola-curee-1872:
Vizetelly and Company issued The Rush for the Spoil at London in 1886, from the thirty-fourth French edition. George Moore wrote the preface to this unabridged English rendering. The French title, La Curee, names the hounds' share of the hunt.

Paris under the Second Empire turns into one vast gamble in these pages. Aristide Saccard, a money man who builds fortunes on fraud, reigns over the dealing. His lovely young wife Renee drifts meanwhile toward scandal and ruin. Greed, luxury, and rot swirl in a fever dream of an age. Few novels catch a corrupt era with such furious energy and color.
nixon-smoking-gun-transcript-1972:
On June 23, 1972, six days after the Watergate break-in, President Richard Nixon met his chief of staff, H. R. Haldeman, in the Oval Office. Their taped talk produced the record later known as the smoking gun. The transcript became public in August 1974, after the Supreme Court ordered the White House to release the tapes.

In the conversation, Nixon approves a plan to have the CIA tell the FBI to back away from its Watergate inquiry, using national security as the excuse. The words proved the president had joined the cover-up from its first week. His support in Congress collapsed within days of the release, and Nixon resigned before the House could vote on impeachment.
cia-0000009672:
Stung Treng province, in Cambodia, is the setting for an April 1972 sighting of two American prisoners of war. Stung Treng sits where Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam nearly meet, along infiltration routes south. Prisoners captured near the trail often passed through this corner.

A sighting here placed captives inside the war's borderland, beyond easy reach or inquiry. Analysts filed it beside other tri-border reports to trace movements. For the two men, the entry may be their only dated trace in Cambodia. The file shows how far the prisoner search stretched past Vietnam itself into Cambodia.
cia-0000010872:
Early in 1951, with Chinese troops fighting Americans in Korea, CIA analysts estimated what the new People's Republic of China could do next. Their paper, dated March 2, 1951, focuses on Chinese Communist capabilities and intentions toward Taiwan, the Soviet Union, and Korea. Beijing had taken power less than two years before, and its aims were still hard to read.

The estimate measures the military reach of Mao's government and weighs where it might strike or hold back. Taiwan, held by the rival Nationalist regime, stood at the center of the question. The paper preserves the moment when Washington first tried to size up its newest major foe.
cia-0000012272:
Sledge writes to Compass in letter number five, a piece of coded correspondence from October 1960 in the Penkovsky operation. The letter concerns an operational guide meant to keep the channel between handlers and their Soviet source working safely. Compass and Sledge are cover names, the cryptonyms officers used in place of real identities on paper.

Behind the code names stood men running mortal risks on both sides of the line. The letter's numbered place in the series shows an operation settling into routine. For readers, it is a working page of tradecraft, written in the flat language of men managing danger.
cia-0000013872: Allied and South Vietnamese prisoners, their treatment, and their trip north fill a CIA note dated August 2, 1967. The note also covers leaflets left on a battlefield. Prisoners of the Saigon government faced the same northward road as Americans. The mix of topics shows how one field report could sweep up many parts of the prison story.
cia-0000014772: How world events struck Italian Jewish circles is the subject of a CIA file dated April 5, 1953. The file mentions the death of Stalin, which had just shaken the world. It likely weighed his passing beside the Rosenberg case's end. The file shows the agency reading mood in one small, watchful community.
cia-0000015272: An unusual phenomenon was seen on the horizon near the Iranian and USSR border, in a CIA report dated August 3, 1966. Horizon sightings were hard to judge, since haze bends light and fools the eye. The border setting still made the report worth filing. It joins the long line of strange lights logged along that tense line.
cia-0000015372: A radio code recording anchors a CIA file dated February 4, 1955. The case name is cut out as deleted in the title. A taped code broadcast could mean a spy channel, a hoax, or a stray signal. The file keeps the puzzle in the set without giving later readers its key.
cia-0000015472: Danish defense leaders took a serious view of flying saucers, the CIA noted in a record dated in 1953. When senior officers treat a topic gravely, staff below them report more freely. Denmark sat on key northern sea lanes, so its skies mattered to allied planners. The entry shows the saucer question earning sober attention in a small allied state.
cia-0000022372: Director McCone ordered a board of inquiry, and the exchange of Powers for Abel is covered in a CIA record dated in 1962. John McCone had just taken over the agency when the swap was made. A board review asked whether the pilot had done his duty. The entry shows the agency judging its own man after judging the enemy's bargain.
cia-0000026872: A Salvadoran military officer stated that only the National Police could do something the clipped title cuts off, in a redacted CIA record dated in 1980. The officer's name was deleted before release. El Salvador was sliding into civil war, and its security forces stood at the center of the storm. A cut statement like this leaves the topic plain and the words gone.
cia-0000028972:
On January 1, 1981, a CIA record noted that the PCD urged an evaluation and revision of the revolution. The short title names the Democratic Conservative Party and its call to rethink the revolutionary course. The record comes from Nicaragua in the early years after the Sandinista victory.

What survives is the party's position as the CIA filed it: a call to stop, review, and change direction. Short records like this still matter, because they fix a party's public stance at a set date. They let later readers trace how political groups shifted as the revolution took shape around them.
cia-0000037172:
The remains of four American pilots were collected in Nghia Binh province, according to a CIA record dated February 1, 1982. Collection of remains was the practical heart of the postwar accounting with Vietnam. Each set of remains raised hopes that names could at last be attached.

The record concerns the gathering of the four pilots' remains in one province. Such work depended on local knowledge of graves and crash sites from the war years. The file shows the recovery effort in its most concrete form. These were not sightings or rumors, but remains in hand. They waited on laboratory work that could give them back their names.
cia-0000045272:
The FMLN-FDR denied contacts on the Ines Duarte kidnapping, in a CIA record dated August 1, 1985. The united front spoke for rebels and their political allies together. A joint denial carried more weight than either part alone could lend.

Inside, the front's disavowal of contacts is preserved as issued. Denying contact is not the same as denying the crime itself. The careful wording left doors open that a flat denial would close. The file holds that careful wording from the case's first days, when every public sentence from every side was shaped to protect a position in secret talks.
cia-0000049272: House intelligence committee staff were briefed in 1991 on reporting about the murder of the Jesuit priests, and a CIA item preserves the session. Staff briefings were where oversight got its facts, away from cameras and speeches. This one shows the agency explaining its own reporting on the case to the people charged with watching it.
cia-0000049372: Dated May 5, 1985, declassified CIA document 0000049372 is headed El Salvador: Terrorist Attack and marked for the Truth Commission. The item concerns a terrorist attack in El Salvador, without naming further detail in its title. It survives as a short dated record of that subject, one of many brief agency notices preserved from the Salvadoran conflict.
cia-0000098272: Possible Chicom Adventure is the terse heading of declassified CIA document 0000098272, dated November 1, 1968. Chicom is period shorthand in the title for Chinese Communist forces. Readers find a short declassified item weighing a possible move, its three-word heading among the briefest in the catalog, giving the feared subject and nothing else.
arxiv-2606-07972: Shelved in the library's PAPERS collection, this 2026 arXiv preprint reports new work. The title's topic is OneFeed: A Unified Generative Framework for Feed Content Enhancement and Query Generation. The backdrop is artificial intelligence (the science of teaching computers to learn from examples and data). The manuscript's gift to the field is a new technique, carefully tested.
arxiv-2606-08072: A research manuscript posted to arXiv in 2026, it contributes new findings. The title declares its subject to be Distance, Normals and Double Normals for real plane Curves with Singularities. The paper works the ground of science and technology — careful study of how the natural and built world works. The manuscript's findings join the public body of research.
arxiv-2606-08372: Among 2026 arXiv preprints, this manuscript stands as a new research report. It takes up the subject named in its title: SoK: Reconstruction Attacks on Synthetic Tabular Data (Insights from Winning the NIST CRC) .... That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
plos-pbio-0000072:
David F. Savage, Pascal F. Egea, Yaneth Robles-Colmenares, and their group solved a protein structure for PLOS Biology in 2003. Their subject is aquaporin Z, a channel in the bacterium E. coli. Aquaporins are pores that let water cross cell membranes fast, while keeping other things out.

Using X-ray methods, the team mapped the channel down to 2.5 angstroms, fine enough to see its shape in detail. The map shows how the pore stays narrow and lined so water passes in single file but ions do not. That design lesson reaches beyond one bacterium. Human aquaporins play roles in the kidney, the eye, and the brain, and their faults cause real disease.
plos-pone-0000072:
Staffan Bensch, Henrik Andrén, Bengt Hansson, and a large team studied a small wolf population in PLOS ONE in 2006. Scandinavian wolves descend from very few founders, so they are highly inbred. Inbreeding usually harms health and breeding, yet this population kept growing.

The team found that wolves choosing mates less related to themselves, keeping offspring more heterozygous, did better. That sorting gives the population some relief from its narrow gene pool. For wildlife managers, the lesson is hopeful but narrow: behavior can soften inbreeding, not erase it. Bringing in new wolves from outside remains the surer cure, and the data help judge when that step is needed.
plos-pone-0000172:
Wook Kim, Tag-Keun Yoo, Sung-Joo Kim, and colleagues published this population genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It tests whether Y-chromosome haplogroups, the family lines traced through fathers, are linked to prostate cancer risk in Korean men. The title gives the result: they found a lack of association.

Negative findings like this one keep the record honest. Many gene-disease links reported in small studies fade when checked in a defined population. The authors genotyped Korean men and compared haplogroup rates between cases and controls. Their null result narrows the search for the genetic roots of prostate cancer in this population.
plos-pone-0000272:
M. Thomas P. Gilbert, Wendy Moore, Linea Melchior, and colleagues published this museum methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Museums hold huge numbers of dry-preserved beetles and other insects whose DNA could serve genetic research, but extracting it used to require damaging the specimen. The authors present a method to extract DNA from dry museum beetles without visible external damage.

Keeping the specimen intact preserves its value for future study. The authors show their method recovers usable DNA while leaving the beetle's outside unchanged. The technique opens museum drawers, some over a century old, to genetic analysis of species that may now be rare or extinct.
plos-pone-0000372:
Mireille Plamondon and colleagues reported on hepatitis C virus infection in Guinea-Bissau in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Hepatitis C spreads mainly through blood, and it often goes unnoticed for years while it harms the liver. The authors examined which strain of the virus circulates in this West African country and how it may be spreading.

The study centers on genotype 2 and raises the possibility that sexual spread plays a role, amplified by exposures involving blood. Knowing how a virus moves through a population shapes screening and prevention plans. The paper adds West African evidence to a disease map drawn mostly from other regions.
plos-pone-0000472:
Bruno Lamontagne and Sherif Abou Elela studied how a cellular cutting enzyme chooses its targets, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The enzyme is eukaryotic RNase III, which cleaves RNA, the cell's message-carrying molecule. The team showed that short RNA guides direct its cleavage, pointing the enzyme to specific spots.

Guided cutting is the principle behind RNA interference, the gene-silencing system that became a major research tool and drug strategy. Showing that short guides steer this enzyme clarifies how cells use small RNAs to control bigger ones. That mechanism underlies both natural gene regulation and engineered attempts to switch off disease genes.
plos-pone-0000572:
Pier Paolo D'Avino and colleagues traced how a key division kinase reaches its post. That post matters at the final step of cell division. Their account appeared in PLOS ONE in 2007. Polo kinase must arrive at the spindle midzone, the bridge between separating chromosome sets, during cytokinesis. The team showed that recruitment of polo kinase there requires the Feo/Klp3A complex, a pair of motor and linker proteins.

Division fails in specific ways when a player misses its cue. Establishing that one complex recruits another orders the cast of cytokinesis into a chain of command. The work was done in fly cells, whose division machinery mirrors our own closely enough to guide human cell biology.
plos-pone-0000672:
Justin G. Boyles and Jonathan J. Storm linked picky eating to extinction risk in bats, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Earlier studies had tied bat extinction risk to two things: smaller geographic range raised it, and habitat specialization raised it too. The authors tested a related hypothesis about diet. Insect-eating bats vary from generalists eating many prey types to specialists eating few.

Their title states the relationship: dietary breadth tracks extinction risk, with narrow eaters in more danger. A specialist starves when its one food source fails, while a generalist can switch. The result gives conservation planners a simple trait to flag at-risk species before populations crash.
plos-pone-0000772:
Coy D. Heldermon, Anne K. Hennig, Kevin K. Ohlemiller and colleagues charted how a storage disease unfolds in mice, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Sanfilippo syndrome type B, also called MPS IIIB, is caused by deficiency of a lysosomal enzyme named Naglu. Children with the disease develop disturbances of sleep, activity, coordination, vision, hearing, and mental functioning, worsening over time.

A mouse model lets researchers watch that progression in sensory, motor, and behavioral deficits in order. Knowing the sequence and timing of decline is essential for testing therapies: a treatment must be given before the damage it hopes to prevent. This natural history in mice sets the benchmarks.
plos-pone-0000872:
Dov Dori and Mordechai Choder argued that clear conceptual models can lead to real findings in systems biology, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Biology now produces facts far faster than any one person can hold in mind. Many modeling tools, they note, struggle to show both structure and behavior at the same time.

To make their case, the authors work through the life cycle of messenger RNA, the copy of a gene that cells use to build proteins. They show how a careful model of that cycle can point to things worth testing in the lab. The article is part method paper, part plea for better shared language.
plos-pone-0000972:
Matthew Hartman, Kristopher Josephson, Chi-Wang Lin and colleagues widened the set of building blocks the ribosome can use, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Ribosomes build proteins from a fixed menu of amino acids. Feeding them unnatural ones could yield huge libraries of modified peptides, rich hunting grounds for new drugs.

The limit is how picky the translation system is about what it accepts. The team present an expanded set of amino acid analogs the ribosome will translate into peptides. Each accepted analog multiplies the shapes a library can take. The work is chemistry groundwork: broaden the menu first, then screen what the new peptides can do.
plos-pone-0001072:
Dan Cojoc, Francesco Difato, Enrico Ferrari and colleagues measured the force exerted by growing cell protrusions, in PLOS ONE in 2007. As neurons differentiate, thin spikes called filopodia and sheets called lamellipodia explore the surroundings. They search for the path the axon should take to its final target.

Their motion had been characterized, but the force they exert was barely known. Force is what lets a growth tip push, pull and test surfaces. The team measured that force and asked which cytoskeletal parts produce it. The cell's skeleton is its muscle and scaffolding in one. Numbers like these turn pictures of growth into mechanics.
plos-pone-0001172:
Finding the variable spots in a genome, called polymorphisms, is easy in humans but hard and costly in species where variation is scarce. Nathalie van Orsouw and colleagues present a method for that problem in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They call it CRoPS, for Complexity Reduction of Polymorphic Sequences.

The approach simplifies complex genomes before sequencing, so large-scale polymorphism discovery becomes practical even in low-variation species. Single nucleotide polymorphisms have revolutionized human medical research, and similar tools could open up breeding and conservation work in plants and animals. The paper describes the method and its intended use.
plos-pone-0001272:
Human bone marrow holds mesenchymal stem cells, which can renew themselves and turn into bone, cartilage, fat, and muscle cells. Atsushi Nagai and colleagues derived a stable human mesenchymal stem cell line from fetal marrow, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. A stable line gives researchers the same cells to work with across many experiments.

The authors report the multilineage potential of the line, testing which tissue types it can still produce. Stem cell lines can drift or lose potency over time, so demonstrating retained potential matters. Such lines are tools for studying development and for regenerative medicine research.
plos-pone-0001372:
Martina Buck and Mario Chojkier wrote a 2007 PLOS ONE study on liver scarring, called fibrosis. When the liver is hurt, star shaped cells wake up and lay down scar tissue. Too much scar tissue can wreck the organ over time. The pair asked which inside cell signals drive this scarring step by step.

The authors show that one signal chain is key for scars to grow. When a certain protein in the star cells is switched on, scarring moves ahead. Long term use of a liver drug also comes into the tests. The work names a clear target for drugs that might slow or stop liver scars.
plos-pone-0001472:
Jie Yang and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a hormone in pikas, small mammals of cold high lands. Pikas do not sleep through winter, so they must cope with harsh cold. Stress from the world can speed change in stress reply proteins. The team traced the hormone leptin across the pika family.

They found marks of strong natural choice on leptin in these cold land pikas. The changes fit a need to burn fuel and hold heat in thin air. Such cases show evolution at work on a known gene. They also hint at how mammals adapt when they settle in extreme homes.
plos-pone-0001572:
Edgar Turner and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on research gaps in oil palm farming. Palm oil groves are often blamed as a top threat to tropical wild life. They sit in some of the richest wild zones on Earth. The team searched the science base for oil palm papers since 1970 and sorted them by topic.

They found wild life checks form a thin share of that work. Most papers chase yield and pests, not species loss. That gap means policy rests on a weak proof base. The study urges a shift in funds toward field checks of real grove impacts.
plos-pone-0001672:
Maria I. Davidich and Stefan Bornholdt built a computer model of the fission yeast cell cycle in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Their model is a Boolean network. Each control protein is treated as simply on or off, and the rules come only from the known wiring of who acts on whom. No numbers were tuned to force the right answer.

When run, the model faithfully reproduced the known order of activity in the real cell cycle of Schizosaccharomyces pombe. The full text gives the network, the rules, and the simulated sequence step by step. That a stripped-down on-off model can replay the cycle suggests the order is built into the wiring itself. That is a useful lesson for modeling other cell circuits.
plos-pone-0001772:
M. Estee Torok and co-authors described HIV-linked tuberculous meningitis in Vietnamese adults in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Tuberculous meningitis, TB infection of the membranes around the brain, is among the deadliest forms of TB, and HIV makes it worse. The study followed patients forward from admission.

Fifty-eight patients were admitted to the study hospital. The team recorded clinical and microbe features, outcomes, and which starting factors predicted death. The full text gives the patient data and the risk factors. Such lists help doctors in busy hospitals spot the patients who need the closest care first.
plos-pone-0001872:

The drug was citalopram, and the data came from the large STAR*D group of patients treated for depression. The genes in view code for the enzymes that clear the drug from the body.

Using a two-stage case and control design, the team split the group in two. They tested whether gene forms tracked with who got better, or who had side effects. As the title states, they found no such link. The null result still helps, since it tells doctors that these genes, at least, do not guide dose choice.
plos-pone-0001972:
Frederique Sauvat and co-authors tested frozen ovary grafts in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Better cancer care now saves more children, but treatment can cost them puberty and fertility. For girls too young for other options, freezing one ovary is the sole path. A few births had already followed grafts of such tissue in women.

The team froze immature mouse ovaries, grafted them back, and watched for puberty and fertility. As the title states, the grafts restored both, and the chemical marks that guide gene use in the young were not altered. That safety point matters for girls who bank tissue before treatment.
plos-pone-0002072:
Anan Yaghmur and co-authors filmed a fat film reshaping itself in real time, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Mixes of two membrane lipids can sit as stacked sheets, called the L alpha phase. The team joined rapid mixing with time-resolved X-ray scattering at a synchrotron, to catch the shift from sheets toward the H2 phase as calcium hits. Watching the change step by step shows how membranes fuse and bend, a basic step in cell life and in drug carrier design.
plos-pone-0002172:
Luc Djogbénou, Fabrice Chandre, Arnaud Berthomieu, and co-authors tracked a pesticide-resistance gene in West African mosquitoes, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The malaria mosquito Anopheles gambiae comes in two molecular forms, called M and S, that are on their way to becoming separate species. Cross-breeding between forms matters because it can move useful traits, such as resistance, from one form to the other.

The team found signs that a resistance change in the ace-1 gene, and a doubling of that gene, had crossed between forms. Such gene flow can speed the spread of insecticide resistance, a serious threat to mosquito control programs that rely on treated nets and sprays.
plos-pone-0002272:
Jae-Hyung Lee, Gloria Culver, Susan Carpenter, and co-authors compared a regulatory RNA element in two lentiviruses, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The team analyzed the EIAV version of the element and found a conserved RNA motif within it. That motif is required for tight binding of Rev in both viruses, despite their distance as relatives. A shared grip point across lentiviruses is useful basic knowledge for anyone designing drugs that block viral replication.

Camilla H. Andreasen, Mette S. Mogensen, Knut Borch-Johnsen and colleagues tested two claimed obesity gene links in a 2008 PLOS ONE study of 18,014 Danes. Earlier genome-wide scans had tied common variants in the genes INSIG2 and PFKP to obesity. Later checks gave mixed answers, so the link was still in doubt.

The Danish data were used to try to confirm, or fail to confirm, those same links in one large group. The title reports non-replication, meaning the earlier links did not hold up here. The study is a useful caution on how gene findings need repeat testing before they can be trusted.
plos-pone-0002972:
R. Maithreye, Ram Sarkar, Veena Parnaik and co-authors modeled delay effects in self-repressing gene circuits in 2008. Every chain of reactions in a cell takes time, from gene expression to daily rhythms. That delay is generic, meaning it shows up in almost all intracellular processes.

In circuits where a gene represses itself, delay can briefly boost expression and create unevenness between cells. The PLOS ONE paper models that transient rise and heterogeneity mathematically. Systems biologists get a clearer sense of when timing alone, without any change in parts, alters cell behavior. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003072:
Carolina Perdigoto, Louis Gervais, Erin Overstreet and co-authors studied unequal protein placement in fly sensory cells in 2008. Unequal division of cell fate determinants is a conserved way to generate diversity in development. In Drosophila, each sensory organ precursor divides into an anterior pIIb and a posterior pIIa cell.

Overexpressing Partner of Numb induced asymmetric distribution of the kinase Skittles in those dividing cells, per the title. Published in PLOS ONE, the detail shows how polarity proteins position the enzymes that mark daughter cell fate, a basic step in building sense organs. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003172:
Gayane P. Manukyan, Karine A. Ghazaryan, Zhanna A. Ktsoyan and colleagues study immune responses to gut microbes in familial Mediterranean fever in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. This autoinflammatory condition brings acute, self-limiting bouts of fever and serositis. It also brings chronic low-grade inflammation even in remission. The team studied what the condition does to levels of these antibodies in the body.

The title reports elevated systemic antibodies toward the normal commensal gut microbiota in this condition. Readers see the gut's usual microbes drawn into a disease passed through families. plos-pone-0003272:
Laura Savolainen, Liana Pusa, Hwa-Jung Kim and colleagues run a pilot tuberculosis test study in Finland in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In recent years, T cell based interferon gamma release assays had been developed for immunodiagnosis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. The pilot study tests diagnostic potential of the recombinant HBHA protein in a vaccinated group in Finland. Readers see a candidate marker tested where BCG vaccination is common. A test that separates active disease from latent infection would change TB care greatly.
plos-pone-0007472: Artemisinin, the malaria drug from sweet wormwood, also kills cancer cells — and this study argues heme, the iron-carrying molecule in blood, is the key. The result points to a shared target behind both the antimalarial and anticancer effects.
plos-pone-0007572: Bone marrow releases progenitor cells that can rebuild blood vessels, but what summons them was unclear. plos-pone-0007672: In a fish where females die after one breeding season, choosing the right mate is everything. This study found females use smell to pick experienced males — the ones most likely to provide good paternal care. Scent becomes a résumé for fatherhood.
plos-pone-0007772: Chickens may pass bird flu to people, so vaccinating poultry matters. This study identified a piece of the H5 flu protein that chicken T cells recognize — and it works across strains. A broadly recognized target is gold for a poultry vaccine.
plos-pone-0007872: Vitamin D's receptor puts the brakes on a cancer-driving pathway. This study showed VDR and vitamin D control expression of TCF-4, a key Wnt-pathway gene, in mouse mammary gland and colon cancer cells. The mechanism links sunshine's vitamin to tumor suppression.
plos-pone-0007972: TB blood tests got a recipe audit. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Smith's team compared ELISpot recipes for TB immune responses. Lab-to-lab results clashed. The key recipe factors were ranked. The audit feeds TB diagnostics.
plos-pone-0008072: Bird flu H5N1 kills through a cytokine storm, while seasonal flu is milder. This study compared the human macrophage response to both viruses at the systems level. The divergent host responses reveal why one flu is a killer and the other a nuisance.
plos-pone-0008172: Allergic asthma was thought to be purely a Th2 disease, but this mouse study found allergen challenge also triggers a Th1 counter-response with interferon-driven GTPases. The self-limiting program suggests the lung tries to brake its own inflammation.
plos-pone-0008272: TB-fighting immune memory was moved between mice. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Duffy's team transferred tuberculosis-specific CD4 T-cell memory and found lingering antigen boosts protection. With BCG's limits clear, new TB vaccines are urgent. The transferred memory held up. The antigen-persistence clue guides next-generation vaccine design.
plos-pone-0008372: A neurodegeneration protein's toxic friendships were mapped. The birds haul the germs across continents. The tick survey maps the airborne route. The finding widens disease surveillance.
plos-pone-0008672: A lung-surfactant protein's key stretch got tested. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Walther's team probed the N-terminal insertion sequence in surfactant protein B analogs. plos-pone-0008772: Women's egg reserve got a birth-to-menopause model. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Wallace and Kelsey modeled the human ovary's egg-follicle count from conception to menopause. The lifetime countdown was charted across the years. The model steers fertility and family-planning care.
plos-pone-0008872: A wasting disease got a vitamin-B2 rescue. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Gonzalez-Cabo's team found flavin adenine dinucleotide rescues frataxin-loss symptoms. The cell-power protein's fuel role was mapped. The vitamin compound restored energy flow. The rescue hints at therapy for the rare disease.
plos-pone-0008972: Lung cancer's CBL gene got a kinase link. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Tan's team showed CBL is frequently altered in lung cancers, relating to MET and EGFR mutations. The ubiquitin ligase's cancer role was mapped. The link informs targeted therapy.
plos-pone-0009072: Bunny antibodies got a human-ready cancer test. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Yu's team humanized a bunny anti-VEGF antibody that starves tumors of vessels in mice. The tuned antibody was checked. The test opens bunny-antibody therapy.
plos-pone-0009172: A virus alarm got a TRAF5 relay. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Tang and Wang showed TRAF5 relays MAVS virus-fighting signals. The RNA-sensing relay was mapped in cells. The relay feeds virus-defense science.
plos-pone-0009272: Computer predictions of immune recognition were shown to need real data. This 2010 PLOS ONE study by Zhang and colleagues exposed limitations of ab initio predictions of peptide binding to MHC class II molecules. While structure-based methods promise to work without large training datasets, the physical-contact evaluations fell short. The finding tempers enthusiasm for purely computational vaccine design.
plos-pone-0009372: Cancer and autism got a shared-typo probe. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Kao's team probed shared typos in cancer and autism. The typo overlap was logged. The probe feeds brain-development science. The overlap spans many genes.
plos-pone-0011472: Mitochondrial optic neuropathy blinds by starving the optic nerve of energy, with no good treatment. This research paper inserts the yeast NDI1 gene — a spare energy enzyme — into rats with the disease and successfully eases their vision loss. Borrowing a yeast gene to patch a mammalian power failure is a bold proof of concept for gene therapy.
plos-pone-0011572: The proteins p73 and p63 are cousins of the famous tumor suppressor p53. This research paper maps their genome-wide binding and finds the two co-occupy target sites with similar DNA-binding profiles. The overlap suggests the siblings share duties in guarding the genome.
plos-pone-0011672: Gammaherpesviruses cause cancers, and they start by dodging the complement system. plos-pone-0011772: Skin cancer thrives where oxygen runs thin, flipping on a survival switch called HIF-1α. This research paper shows the protein Bcl-2 keeps that switch stable in starved melanoma cells, with help from the chaperone HSP90. The support chain reveals how tumors endure suffocation.
